RL.questionText: What does little bear do when he feels cold?
RL.passage: Little bear woke up one morning and felt very cold. He looked outside and saw snow on the ground. He grabbed his favorite red blanket and curled up by the fireplace. His mother brought him a warm cup of honey tea. Little bear smiled and felt much better.

options.text: He grabbed his blanket and sat by the fire
He went outside to play in the snow
He asked his mother to go to the store
He went back to sleep in his bed

RL.explanation: The passage says little bear grabbed his red blanket and curled up by the fireplace when he felt cold.

RL.questionText: Where does most of this story take place?
RL.passage: The twins ran down the hill and jumped into the big pile of leaves their father had raked. Crunch! The leaves scattered everywhere. Their dog, Biscuit, barked and leaped in after them. Dad laughed and shook his head. 'I guess I'll be raking again,' he said. The backyard smelled like autumn.

options.text: In the family's backyard
At a park near the school
Inside the family's house
At a neighbor's yard down the street

RL.explanation: Details like 'backyard,' 'their father,' and 'Dad' all point to the family's own backyard as the setting.

RL.questionText: What problem does Amara face at the beginning of the story?
RL.passage: Amara had been looking forward to soccer tryouts all week. But on the morning of tryouts, she woke up with a sore throat and a headache. Her mom felt her forehead. 'No tryouts today,' Mom said firmly. Amara stared at the ceiling, fighting back tears. She had practiced every day for a month.

options.text: She gets sick the morning of the tryouts she had prepared for
She forgot to practice for the tryouts
Her mother will not let her join the soccer team
She wakes up late and misses the tryouts

RL.explanation: Amara's problem is that she falls ill on tryout day after a month of practice — classic story-structure problem setup.

RL.questionText: What is the central message of this passage?
RL.passage: Maya had practiced her violin every day for six months, but at the recital she forgot her notes halfway through and ran offstage crying. Her grandfather found her. 'I saw someone brave enough to stand on that stage,' he said. 'The music you practiced lives in your hands. Come back tomorrow and play it just for me.' Maya wiped her tears. The next evening, she played flawlessly.

options.text: Mistakes are part of learning, and persistence leads to growth
Recitals are too stressful for young musicians
Grandparents always give the best advice about music
Practicing every day guarantees a perfect performance

RL.explanation: The grandfather's encouragement and Maya's eventual success after failure communicate that mistakes are learning opportunities.

RL.questionText: Which detail best shows that Darius is nervous before his speech?
RL.passage: Darius stared at the index cards in his hand. He had written his speech three times and memorized every word, but now the gym seemed enormous. Two hundred faces looked up at him from the bleachers. He cleared his throat and looked at the floor. 'You've got this,' his teacher whispered from the wings. Darius took a slow breath, lifted his eyes, and began.

options.text: He stares at the floor and clears his throat before speaking
He had memorized his speech before getting to the gym
His teacher is standing in the wings of the stage
There are two hundred people in the bleachers

RL.explanation: Looking at the floor and clearing his throat are behavioral cues that directly signal Darius's nervousness.

RL.questionText: The passage is narrated from Marcus's point of view. How would the story be different if narrated by Jayla?
RL.passage: Marcus watched Jayla walk to the front to accept the science fair trophy. He told himself he wasn't jealous — his project had just had bad luck when the battery died. He clapped politely. Later, Jayla sat next to him at lunch. 'Your idea was actually cooler than mine,' she said quietly. Marcus stared at his tray. He hadn't expected that.

options.text: Readers would learn what Jayla felt about winning and why she spoke to Marcus
The events of the story would happen in a different order
Marcus would be described as a much stronger student
The story would be set in a different location

RL.explanation: Point of view determines whose inner thoughts we access; shifting to Jayla would reveal her feelings about winning and her reason for complimenting Marcus.

RL.questionText: What does 'trepidation' most likely mean as used in the passage?
RL.passage: Dominique approached the stage with trepidation, her palms sweating and her breath coming in shallow bursts. She had rehearsed her spoken word poem over a hundred times in her bedroom mirror, but standing before four hundred people felt entirely different. The lights were blinding. She gripped the microphone and told herself: just breathe.

options.text: A feeling of fear or nervousness about something that might happen
Great excitement and eagerness to begin
A sense of pride in one's past accomplishments
Confusion about where to stand or what to do

RL.explanation: Context clues like 'palms sweating,' 'shallow bursts,' and 'blinding lights' all point to anxiety and fear — the meaning of trepidation.

RL.questionText: How does the author use the storm setting to develop the narrator's internal conflict?
RL.passage: The rain came down in sheets by the time I reached the bridge. Below, the river moved fast and dark — nothing like the lazy summer water where Rosa and I had once floated on inflatable rafts and argued over who had a better playlist. That was before. I stood at the railing, hood soaked through, unable to cross to her side of town and unable to go back.

options.text: The violent storm mirrors the narrator's inability to move forward or go back in the relationship
The storm is used only to show that the weather is bad that evening
The setting proves that the narrator and Rosa used to be enemies
The rain forces the narrator to think about buying better rain gear

RL.explanation: The storm and swollen river mirror the narrator's emotional paralysis — they literally cannot cross, reflecting their inability to resolve the conflict with Rosa.

RL.questionText: Why does Sofia decide to keep the bird?
RL.passage: Sofia found the small sparrow in the garden with a hurt wing. She put it in a shoebox with a soft cloth and some seeds. Every day after school she checked on it and gave it fresh water. After two weeks, the wing healed. Sofia opened the box outside, but the bird just hopped around her feet. It did not fly away. Her mom smiled. 'I think you have a friend,' she said.

options.text: The bird stays near her even after it is healed and able to leave
Her mom tells her she must keep the bird as a pet
The bird's wing does not fully heal and it cannot fly
Sofia put the bird back in the shoebox when it would not fly

RL.explanation: The bird chooses to stay near Sofia even after healing — it hops around her feet rather than flying away.

RL.questionText: How does the author structure this passage to build suspense?
RL.passage: The hallway was silent except for the hum of the fluorescent light overhead. Kenji pressed himself against the wall and listened. There it was again: a soft scraping sound from behind the locked door at the end of the corridor. He had been told that room was empty. The school had been told that room was empty for fifteen years. He reached for the handle.

options.text: By layering sensory details and a contradiction between what Kenji was told and what he hears
By describing the school in detail from beginning to end
By using flashbacks to explain why the room was locked
By comparing two different characters' reactions to the sound

RL.explanation: The author builds suspense through sensory details (hum, scraping) and the contradiction between 'empty room' and the unexplained sound.

RL.questionText: How does the cat feel at the end of the story?
RL.passage: The cat hid under the bed when it heard thunder. It shook and would not come out. Then the thunder stopped. The sun came back out. The cat walked out slowly and sat in the sunny spot by the window. It purred and closed its eyes.

options.text: Calm and happy in the sun
Still scared of the thunder
Hungry and looking for food
Angry at the loud noise

RL.explanation: After the storm the cat purrs and closes its eyes in the sunny window — signs of feeling calm and content.

RL.questionText: How does the setting in the passage affect how the character feels?
RL.passage: Zara had never seen so many stars. Her family had driven far from the city to a dark meadow in the mountains. She lay on her back in the cool grass and looked up. The stars seemed close enough to touch. She let out a slow breath. All week she had worried about the math test. But tonight, under that enormous sky, her worries seemed very small.

options.text: Being under the vast night sky makes her worries feel less important
The dark meadow makes her feel afraid and unsafe
The stars remind her to study harder for the math test
Being in the mountains makes her miss her home in the city

RL.explanation: The passage says 'under that enormous sky, her worries seemed very small' — the setting creates a sense of perspective that relieves her anxiety.

RL.questionText: What does 'reluctantly' most likely mean in this sentence from the passage?
RL.passage: Jaylen wanted to spend Saturday playing video games. But his mother reminded him that they had promised to help Grandma in her garden. Jaylen reluctantly put down his controller, laced up his old sneakers, and followed his mom to the car. An hour later, digging in the warm dirt with Grandma telling stories, he was glad he had come.

options.text: Unwillingly, without enthusiasm
Quickly and without thinking
Happily and with excitement
Carelessly and without paying attention

RL.explanation: Jaylen wanted to play games but had to stop — reluctantly means doing something unwillingly, which fits the context.

RL.questionText: What causes the change in Priya's character by the end of the passage?
RL.passage: Priya had always believed she was not athletic. She avoided gym class and spent recesses reading. When her teacher paired her with Destiny for the relay race, she expected humiliation. But Destiny coached her patiently through each practice — 'lean forward, pump your arms' — until Priya's form improved. On race day, Priya ran her leg faster than she ever expected. For the first time, she wondered what else she had been wrong about herself.

options.text: Patient coaching and one surprising success cause Priya to question her self-limiting beliefs
Winning the relay race convinces Priya she should become a professional runner
Being paired with a fast partner means Priya does not need to try hard
Priya's teacher forces her to change her attitude about sports

RL.explanation: Destiny's patient coaching and Priya's unexpected strong performance together shift her belief about her own abilities.

RL.questionText: Which quote from the passage BEST supports the idea that the narrator is starting to accept the move?
RL.passage: For three months after we moved, I refused to unpack my room. My boxes stood stacked like a protest — I wasn't staying, so why pretend? But last week I found my old poster of the constellations buried at the bottom of one. I taped it to the ceiling above my bed. I still miss home. But maybe this ceiling can be mine too.

options.text: 'I taped it to the ceiling above my bed... maybe this ceiling can be mine too.'
'My boxes stood stacked like a protest — I wasn't staying, so why pretend?'
'For three months after we moved, I refused to unpack my room.'
'I still miss home.'

RL.explanation: Hanging the poster is a small act of claiming the new space; 'maybe this ceiling can be mine' directly expresses tentative acceptance.

RL.questionText: What tone does the author create in this passage, and how?
RL.passage: The championship trophy sat in the glass case for fifteen years, gathering dust. The school had won it in a year nobody quite remembered, for a sport the district no longer offered, coached by a man whose name had been spelled wrong on the plaque. Every September the janitor polished it dutifully. Every September no one noticed.

options.text: Ironic and melancholy, through the contrast between the trophy's symbolic importance and its total neglect
Triumphant and proud, by describing the school's athletic achievement
Angry and accusatory, by blaming the school for forgetting its history
Humorous and light, because the misspelled plaque is funny

RL.explanation: The details — dust, forgotten sport, misspelled name, unnoticed polishing — create irony and melancholy: something meant to commemorate is itself forgotten.

RL.questionText: What does Max bring to show the class?
RL.passage: Max was excited for show-and-tell day. He put his pet rock in a paper bag and brought it to school. When it was his turn, he held it up for everyone to see. 'This rock is from the river near my grandpa's house,' he said. 'It is smooth because the water rolled it for many years.' His classmates wanted to hold it.

options.text: A smooth rock from the river near his grandfather's house
A photo of his grandfather's house
A jar of river water
A fish he caught at the river

RL.explanation: Max brings a pet rock that came from the river near his grandpa's house — a smooth river rock.

RL.questionText: Both passages feature a character facing a challenge alone. How do the themes differ?
RL.passage: Passage A: Eli climbed the last ledge alone, legs shaking. No one had believed he could summit without a guide. He planted his flag and felt a fierce, private joy. He needed no one's approval — only the mountain had ever truly understood him. Passage B: Amara waited on the far side of the rope bridge, calling encouragement across the gorge. When her friend Lena finally made it across, both of them cheered. 'We did it,' Lena breathed. 'No,' Amara said, smiling. 'You did it. I just believed.'

options.text: Passage A emphasizes self-reliance; Passage B emphasizes how belief from others enables personal achievement
Both passages argue that individual effort is the only path to success
Passage A is about physical challenges; Passage B is about emotional ones
Both passages show that friendship is more important than personal goals

RL.explanation: Eli's success is solitary and self-affirming; Lena's success is enabled by Amara's belief — the themes differ on isolation vs. supported growth.

RL.questionText: What does the dialogue reveal about the relationship between the two characters?
RL.passage: 'You don't have to come,' Rashida said, not looking up from her laces. 'I know I don't.' Marcus leaned against the doorframe. 'I want to.' She finally looked at him. 'You always say that.' 'And I always show up.' She said nothing for a moment, then pulled on her jacket. 'Fine. But don't talk the whole way.' He smiled. 'Wouldn't dream of it.'

options.text: Comfortable and long-standing — their banter suggests trust beneath the surface tension
Hostile and deteriorating — Rashida clearly wants Marcus to leave her alone
Formal and professional — they are colleagues who don't know each other well
Competitive and jealous — they are rivals trying to get an advantage over each other

RL.explanation: Rashida's 'You always say that' and Marcus's 'And I always show up' shows a pattern of reliability; her grudging acceptance reveals trust beneath the surface.

RL.questionText: Based on the passage, which detail tells you the most about what kind of person Grandma Chen is?
RL.passage: Grandma Chen's kitchen smelled like ginger and something frying. She never used recipes — she said her hands remembered the measurements. On the refrigerator door were photos: graduations, weddings, babies, and one faded picture of a young woman standing in front of a factory with her chin raised. 'Is that you?' Lena asked. Grandma Chen smiled and turned back to the stove. 'That was the day I stopped being afraid,' she said.

options.text: The photo and her words about it show she has faced fear and come through it with quiet pride
She uses no recipes, which shows she is disorganized in the kitchen
Having many family photos shows she is proud only of her family's achievements
The smell of the kitchen tells us she cooks the same food every day

RL.explanation: The factory photo and 'the day I stopped being afraid' reveal a woman who faced a difficult challenge and emerged with resilience and quiet confidence.

RI.questionText: According to the passage, where do monarch butterflies go in fall?
RI.passage: Monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles every year. In fall, they fly south to warmer places in Mexico. They cannot survive cold winters in the north. In spring, they fly back north to lay their eggs on milkweed plants. Scientists study these butterflies to learn how they find their way.

options.text: They fly south to warmer places in Mexico
They hide underground until spring
They fly north to find milkweed plants
Scientists move them to warmer states

RI.explanation: The passage states directly that monarchs 'fly south to warmer places in Mexico' in the fall.

RI.questionText: Why did the author most likely write this passage?
RI.passage: Sea turtles have lived on Earth for more than 100 million years. They can hold their breath for up to seven hours. Female sea turtles travel back to the same beach where they were born to lay their eggs. Sadly, many sea turtles are endangered because of pollution and fishing nets. People around the world are working to protect them.

options.text: To inform readers about sea turtles and the need to protect them
To entertain readers with a made-up story about a sea turtle
To teach readers how to catch sea turtles safely
To convince readers that all fishing should be banned

RI.explanation: The passage shares facts about sea turtles and ends with the problem they face and efforts to help — the author's purpose is to inform and raise awareness.

RI.questionText: What is the main idea of this passage?
RI.passage: Hip-hop music began in the South Bronx neighborhood of New York City in the 1970s. DJs like DJ Kool Herc discovered they could extend the drum break of a song by switching between two copies of the same record. This created space for dancers — called b-boys and b-girls — to show their moves. MCs began speaking rhythmically over the beats. What started as a block party tradition grew into a global art form that shapes fashion, language, and music worldwide.

options.text: Hip-hop originated in New York and grew into a worldwide cultural force
DJs are the most important part of hip-hop music
Hip-hop dancing requires years of practice to learn
Block parties in the 1970s were popular in New York

RI.explanation: The passage traces hip-hop from its South Bronx origins to global influence — that arc is the main idea.

RI.questionText: Which text feature would BEST help find where jaguars live in a rainforest article?
RI.passage: An article about rainforests includes the following features: a map showing where tropical rainforests are located around the world; a sidebar listing facts about annual rainfall; bold vocabulary words like 'canopy,' 'understory,' and 'biodiversity'; and section headings such as 'Rainforest Plants,' 'Rainforest Animals,' and 'Threats to Rainforests.'

options.text: The map showing rainforest regions
The sidebar facts about rainfall
The bold vocabulary definitions
The heading titled 'Rainforest Plants'

RI.explanation: A map showing geographic regions would most directly show where jaguars live.

RI.questionText: What connection exists between deforestation and indigenous communities?
RI.passage: The Amazon rainforest is home to more than 400 indigenous groups who have lived there for thousands of years. These communities depend on the forest for food, medicine, and cultural practices. Deforestation driven by logging and cattle ranching has destroyed millions of acres of forest, displacing communities and erasing traditional knowledge developed over generations. Scientists note that many of these communities have identified plant compounds that later became important medicines.

options.text: Deforestation destroys the land and knowledge that indigenous communities depend on
Indigenous communities benefit from increased trade due to deforestation
Deforestation only affects the wildlife, not the people living in the Amazon
Indigenous groups have recently moved to cities to avoid deforestation

RI.explanation: The passage directly connects deforestation to displacement of communities and loss of traditional knowledge.

RI.questionText: Which sentence best supports the claim that plastic pollution harms ocean ecosystems?
RI.passage: Each year, roughly 8 million metric tons of plastic enter the world's oceans. Sea turtles often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and ingest them, causing fatal blockages. Microplastics have been found in the digestive systems of over 700 marine species. Researchers at the Ocean Health Institute found that coral reef ecosystems exposed to plastic show a 20-fold increase in disease susceptibility. Recycling programs have expanded, but experts argue that production cuts are necessary to meaningfully reduce ocean plastic.

options.text: Coral reef ecosystems exposed to plastic show a 20-fold increase in disease susceptibility
Recycling programs have expanded in recent years
Experts argue that production cuts are necessary
Roughly 8 million metric tons of plastic enter oceans each year

RI.explanation: The coral reef statistic directly demonstrates harm to an ocean ecosystem with specific, quantified evidence.

RI.questionText: Based on the passage, what does 'neuroplasticity' most likely mean?
RI.passage: For many years, scientists believed the brain was fixed after early childhood. Recent research has overturned that idea. Neuroplasticity — the brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life — has been observed in people recovering from strokes, learning new languages, and even in musicians who practice daily. These findings suggest that deliberate practice can physically reshape the brain's structure.

options.text: The brain's ability to change and form new connections throughout life
The process by which the brain stops developing after childhood
A medical condition that affects memory and learning
The speed at which nerve signals travel through the body

RI.explanation: The passage defines neuroplasticity directly as 'the brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life.'

RI.questionText: What is the author's most likely purpose in including the statistic about internet usage?
RI.passage: In 2023, the global average daily internet use reached nearly seven hours per person. Researchers studying adolescent health note that heavy social media use correlates with increased reports of anxiety and loneliness, particularly in girls ages 11–14. However, internet access has also enabled millions of students in remote areas to access educational resources previously unavailable to them. The debate over technology use reflects a deeper tension between connection and distraction.

options.text: To establish the scale of internet use before exploring its complex effects
To prove that internet use is always harmful to young people
To convince readers to reduce their time online immediately
To show that internet use has no effect on mental health

RI.explanation: The statistic anchors the discussion — it establishes how pervasive internet use is before the author examines both its benefits and drawbacks.

RI.questionText: What caused the bee population to decrease?
RI.passage: Bees are important pollinators. Without bees, many plants cannot make seeds. In recent years, the number of bees has gone down. Scientists believe this happened because of pesticides used on crops, loss of wildflowers, and diseases spread by tiny mites. Farmers are now planting wildflower strips around fields to help bees find food.

options.text: Pesticides, loss of wildflowers, and mite diseases
Too many bees working in the same area
Farmers stopped growing crops that bees like
Bees moved to cities where there are no plants

RI.explanation: The passage lists three causes: pesticides, loss of wildflowers, and mite diseases.

RI.questionText: Which detail best explains why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids?
RI.passage: The ancient Egyptians built the pyramids as tombs for their pharaohs. Pharaohs were believed to be gods on Earth, and Egyptians believed their rulers would continue their divine role in the afterlife. The pyramids were designed to protect the body and treasures buried inside. The Great Pyramid of Giza took approximately 20 years to build and required tens of thousands of workers. Inside, complex passageways were meant to confuse tomb robbers.

options.text: Pharaohs were believed to be gods who would continue their role in the afterlife
Egypt needed large buildings to show how powerful it was compared to other countries
The pyramids were built to provide work for thousands of Egyptian citizens
Egyptians built pyramids to study the movements of the stars

RI.explanation: The passage states that pyramids were built to house pharaohs believed to be divine so they could continue their role in the afterlife.

RI.questionText: What is this passage mostly about?
RI.passage: Dogs use their noses to learn about the world. A dog's nose is much stronger than a human's nose. Dogs can smell things that are very far away. Police dogs use their noses to help find missing people. Some dogs can even smell when a person is sick. Dogs are amazing animals.

options.text: How dogs use their powerful sense of smell
Why police officers need dogs
How dogs are trained to find food
Why dogs are better pets than cats

RI.explanation: The whole passage is about dogs' remarkable sense of smell and how they use it.

RI.questionText: A student is reading about the water cycle. What would a diagram showing how water moves from clouds to ocean to clouds help the reader do?
RI.passage: The water cycle describes how water moves continuously through Earth's environments. Water evaporates from oceans and lakes, rises as water vapor, cools to form clouds, and falls back to Earth as rain or snow. This process has been happening for billions of years and is essential to all life on Earth. Scientists use diagrams and models to help explain the stages of this cycle.

options.text: See the sequence and movement of the water cycle stages more clearly
Find the definition of the word 'evaporate'
Understand how scientists discovered the water cycle
Identify which countries get the most rain

RI.explanation: A visual diagram of movement helps readers understand sequence and process — exactly what the water cycle involves.

RI.questionText: Which sentence from the passage provides the strongest evidence for the author's argument?
RI.passage: Many experts believe that schools should start later in the morning. Research shows that teenagers' biological clocks naturally shift to later sleep and wake times. A study of 30,000 students in Minneapolis found that when school start times moved from 7:15 a.m. to 8:40 a.m., grades improved and car crashes among teen drivers dropped by 70 percent. Some parents worry about childcare logistics, but researchers argue the academic and safety benefits outweigh those concerns.

options.text: 'Grades improved and car crashes among teen drivers dropped by 70 percent'
'Many experts believe that schools should start later in the morning'
'Some parents worry about childcare logistics'
'Teenagers' biological clocks naturally shift to later sleep and wake times'

RI.explanation: Specific quantified outcomes (grade improvements + 70% drop in crashes) provide the strongest, most concrete evidence.

RI.questionText: How do the two sources differ in their claim about social media and creativity?
RI.passage: Source 1: A 2022 survey found that 68% of teen artists reported discovering their art style through social media platforms, where exposure to diverse creators accelerated their creative development. Source 2: A developmental psychology study argues that constant exposure to others' finished work discourages experimentation: teens who spend more than two hours daily consuming art content produce fewer original works than peers who limit their social media use.

options.text: Source 1 says social media accelerates creative discovery; Source 2 says it discourages original work
Both sources agree that social media always helps teen creativity
Source 1 focuses on psychology; Source 2 focuses on statistics
Source 2 claims social media is essential for all creative development

RI.explanation: Source 1 shows discovery and acceleration; Source 2 shows discouragement of experimentation — directly conflicting claims.

RI.questionText: How is the passage organized, and how does that structure support the author's purpose?
RI.passage: Before 1900, fewer than 1,000 bison remained in North America — down from an estimated 30–60 million a century earlier. Targeted hunting, habitat destruction, and government policies aimed at displacing Indigenous peoples drove them to near extinction. In 1905, the American Bison Society launched coordinated breeding and reintroduction programs. By 2023, the North American bison population had recovered to approximately 500,000. The recovery demonstrates what targeted conservation can accomplish when political will and scientific expertise align.

options.text: Chronologically — moving from crisis to cause to intervention to recovery, showing that conservation action produced measurable results
Compare/contrast — showing how bison today are different from bison in 1900
Problem/solution repeated twice, with no clear connection between the two cycles
Order of importance — with the most important facts listed first

RI.explanation: The passage follows a clear timeline: near-extinction (before 1900), causes, intervention (1905), recovery (2023) — chronological structure supporting a conservation-works argument.

RI.questionText: Look at the passage. What would a chart showing how tall different trees grow help you understand?
RI.passage: Trees grow to many different heights. The coast redwood is the tallest tree in the world. Some redwoods grow taller than 350 feet. Oak trees are much shorter. Most oaks grow between 60 and 100 feet tall. Apple trees are even smaller — most are about 20 feet tall. A chart can help compare the heights of different types of trees.

options.text: How the heights of different trees compare to each other
How old the different trees are
Where in the world each type of tree grows
How many leaves each type of tree has

RI.explanation: A height chart lets you compare the sizes of redwoods, oaks, and apple trees side by side.

RI.questionText: What is the author's main purpose in this passage?
RI.passage: Every year, millions of pounds of food are thrown away in the United States. Much of this food is still safe to eat. Food banks and shelters need donations. If every family saved their leftovers and donated extra food, fewer people would go hungry. We can all help solve the problem of food waste and hunger at the same time.

options.text: To persuade readers to take action to reduce food waste and help people who are hungry
To describe how food banks operate and find volunteers
To inform readers about which foods go bad most quickly
To entertain readers with a story about a food bank worker

RI.explanation: The passage ends with 'We can all help' — a call to action that shows the author's persuasive intent.

RI.questionText: According to the passage, what happened as a result of the invention of the printing press?
RI.passage: Before the printing press was invented in the 1440s, books were written by hand and very expensive. Only wealthy people and church officials could afford them. Johannes Gutenberg's invention made it possible to print many copies of a book quickly and cheaply. Within 50 years, millions of books had been printed across Europe. Literacy rates began to rise as more people could afford to learn to read. The spread of ideas through books contributed to major changes in science, religion, and government.

options.text: Books became affordable, literacy rose, and ideas spread widely across Europe
Only wealthy people were able to buy books from the new printing machines
The church gained more control over who could read and learn
Writing by hand became more popular as a skilled art form

RI.explanation: The passage chains the effects: printing press → cheaper books → higher literacy → spread of ideas.

RI.questionText: Which sentence from the passage tells you why the giant panda was taken off the endangered species list?
RI.passage: Giant pandas were once critically endangered. In the wild, they survive only by eating bamboo — up to 40 pounds per day. Habitat loss and low birth rates made recovery difficult. But decades of conservation work paid off. Protected forest reserves were expanded in China, and breeding programs in zoos helped increase the population. By 2021, China officially removed the giant panda from its endangered species list, noting that wild populations had grown to over 1,800 animals.

options.text: 'Wild populations had grown to over 1,800 animals'
'Giant pandas were once critically endangered'
'They survive only by eating bamboo — up to 40 pounds per day'
'Habitat loss and low birth rates made recovery difficult'

RI.explanation: The population growth figure directly explains the decision to remove pandas from the endangered list.

RI.questionText: A student reads a written article and watches a documentary about climate change. What can the documentary show that the written article cannot?
RI.passage: A written news article about Arctic ice loss describes the rate of melting using statistics and quotes from scientists. A documentary on the same topic includes footage of glaciers calving into the ocean, interviews with Inuit community members whose villages are flooding, and time-lapse video showing decades of ice retreat compressed into seconds. Both cover the same scientific facts, but the experiences they create for the audience are different.

options.text: Visual and emotional impact through footage and time-lapse that makes the scale of change viscerally clear
More accurate scientific data than written articles can include
A longer and more detailed explanation of the scientific process
An unbiased view because documentaries cannot include opinions

RI.explanation: The passage explains that the documentary's footage and time-lapse create a different audience experience — visual and emotional impact that text cannot replicate.

RF.questionText: Which word rhymes with 'cat'?

options.text: bat
cup
dog
ship

RF.explanation: 'Bat' ends in the same -at sound as 'cat,' making them rhyming words.

RF.questionText: When reading a book in English, where do you begin reading on a page?

options.text: At the top left, moving right across each line
At the bottom of the page, moving upward
In the middle of the page, moving outward
At the top right, moving left across each line

RF.explanation: In English, text is read left-to-right, top-to-bottom.

RF.questionText: Which word contains a long 'a' sound spelled with a silent 'e'?

options.text: cake
clap
grab
flat

RF.explanation: 'Cake' follows the CVCe pattern — the silent 'e' makes the 'a' say its long vowel name.

RF.questionText: Which word uses the 'igh' pattern to make a long 'i' sound?

options.text: night
nice
nine
bite

RF.explanation: 'Night' uses the 'igh' trigraph to spell the long 'i' sound.

RF.questionText: A student reads smoothly, at the right speed, and with expression. This is called —

options.text: fluency
decoding
phonemic awareness
summarizing

RF.explanation: Fluency is reading with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression.

RF.questionText: How many syllables does the word 'celebration' have?
RF.explanation: Cel-e-bra-tion has four syllables.

RF.questionText: What new word do you get if you take away the /b/ in 'blend' and replace it with /fr/?

options.text: frend (friend sound)
lend
fend
frond

RF.explanation: Replacing /bl/ with /fr/ in 'blend' gives the 'frend' sound — onset substitution.

RF.questionText: A student reads 'photo' as 'p-hot-o.' What should the student do?

options.text: Recognize 'ph' as a digraph that makes the /f/ sound
Look up the word in a dictionary before reading
Skip the word and come back to it later
Replace it with a word that looks similar

RF.explanation: 'Ph' is a consonant digraph that makes the /f/ sound. Recognizing digraphs helps decode words fluently.

RF.questionText: Which pair of words begins with the same sound?

options.text: ship / shell
ball / call
tree / free
pan / ban

RF.explanation: 'Ship' and 'shell' both begin with the /sh/ digraph sound.

RF.questionText: Which word has a short 'o' sound in the middle?

options.text: hop
hope
home
hose

RF.explanation: 'Hop' has a short /o/ sound. The others use CVCe pattern making a long vowel.

RF.questionText: What is the vowel sound in 'rain' called?

options.text: Long a, spelled ai
Short a, spelled ai
Long e, spelled ai
Short i, spelled ai

RF.explanation: The vowel team 'ai' makes the long /a/ sound in 'rain' — when two vowels go walking, the first one does the talking.

RF.questionText: What is the purpose of a period at the end of a sentence?

options.text: It signals the end of a complete thought and tells the reader to pause
It shows the reader that a new character is speaking
It means the sentence is a question
It tells the reader to read the next sentence louder

RF.explanation: Periods mark the end of a declarative sentence — a complete thought — and signal a full stop pause in reading.

RF.questionText: The word 'unhappiness' can be broken into smaller parts. Which correctly shows its prefix, root, and suffix?

options.text: un- (prefix) + happy (root) + -ness (suffix)
unhapy + ness
un + happiness
unhappy + iness

RF.explanation: 'Unhappiness' = un- (not) + happy (root) + -ness (state of being). Breaking words into morphemes aids decoding and meaning.

RF.questionText: Which pair of words are homophones (sound the same but are spelled differently)?

options.text: knight / night
knot / not looking alike
write / right / both
their / there / they're (all three)

RF.explanation: 'Knight' and 'night' are pronounced identically but spelled differently — classic homophones. (Note: 'their/there/they're' are homophones too, but option D is the cleanest single pair.)

RF.questionText: A student reads slowly and sounds out every word one letter at a time. What strategy would most help increase fluency?

options.text: Practice reading familiar texts repeatedly until the words become automatic
Focus only on reading harder and harder new texts each day
Read only silently so there is no pressure to sound good
Skip words that are hard and never go back to them

RF.explanation: Repeated reading of familiar texts builds automaticity — the ability to recognize words instantly without sounding them out — which is the foundation of fluency.

RF.questionText: Which word is spelled correctly when adding the suffix -ing to 'run'?

options.text: running
runing
runnning
runeing

RF.explanation: When adding -ing to a single-syllable word ending in consonant-vowel-consonant (CVC), double the final consonant: run → running.

RF.questionText: Which letter makes the first sound in the word 'fish'?

options.text: f
p
v
b

RF.explanation: 'Fish' begins with the /f/ sound, spelled with the letter f.

RF.questionText: Which word uses the 'ow' vowel team to make the long /o/ sound?

options.text: snow
now
cow
how

RF.explanation: 'Snow' uses 'ow' to make the long /o/ sound. 'Now,' 'cow,' and 'how' use 'ow' to make the /ow/ diphthong instead.

RF.questionText: How many phonemes (sounds) are in the word 'ship'?
RF.explanation: 'Ship' has 3 phonemes: /sh/ + /ĭ/ + /p/. The letters 's' and 'h' together make one sound.

RF.questionText: What does the prefix 'pre-' most commonly mean?

options.text: before
again
not
across

RF.explanation: The prefix 'pre-' means 'before': preview, preheat, predict. Knowing prefixes is a key word recognition strategy.

W.questionText: Which sentence states a clear opinion for an essay about pets?

options.text: Dogs make the best pets because they are loyal and help keep their owners active.
Some people have dogs and some people have cats.
My neighbor has a goldfish in a bowl by the window.
Animals come in many different shapes and sizes.

W.explanation: An opinion sentence states a position ('make the best pets') and includes a reason ('loyal' and 'keep owners active').

W.questionText: Which sentence would make the BEST opening for an essay arguing schools should have longer recess?

options.text: Schools should give students at least 45 minutes of recess every day because physical activity helps kids learn better.
Recess is the time of day when students go outside to play.
Some schools have long recess and some schools have short recess.
I like recess because it is fun to play with my friends.

W.explanation: A strong opinion opening states the writer's position clearly and gives a reason — option A does both.

W.questionText: Which sentence works best as a topic sentence for an informative paragraph about volcanoes?

options.text: Volcanoes are powerful geological formations that can dramatically reshape the landscape around them.
Lava can flow at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour on steep slopes.
I think volcanoes are the most interesting natural disaster.
The word 'volcano' comes from the Roman god Vulcan.

W.explanation: A topic sentence introduces the main idea broadly. Option A introduces volcanoes as a subject for the whole paragraph; the others are details or opinions.

W.questionText: Which sentence uses the most vivid detail for a story about a storm?

options.text: The thunder cracked so loudly that the windows rattled and my dog scrambled under the bed.
There was a big storm outside.
The storm happened at night and it was loud.
My family stayed inside because of the weather.

W.explanation: Vivid narrative writing uses sensory details and specific actions — option A gives readers sound and movement.

W.questionText: A student wrote: 'The author argues that social media harms teen mental health.' Which addition best supports this claim with text evidence?

options.text: According to the article, 'teens who spend more than 3 hours daily on social media are twice as likely to report feelings of depression.'
Many teenagers use social media to stay in touch with friends.
In my opinion, social media can be both good and bad for young people.
The author wrote this article for a health magazine.

W.explanation: Text evidence means quoting or paraphrasing from the source with a specific, relevant statistic.

W.questionText: A student is writing a research report about climate change. Which source would be MOST reliable?

options.text: A peer-reviewed article by climate scientists published in a scientific journal
A comment from an anonymous poster on a social media site
A blog post from a travel website about vacation weather
A five-year-old encyclopedia entry without cited sources

W.explanation: Peer-reviewed scientific journals are the most reliable because they involve expert review and use cited evidence.

W.questionText: Which revision makes this claim MOST persuasive? Original: 'School uniforms are a good idea.'

options.text: School uniforms reduce socioeconomic pressure and allow students to focus on learning rather than clothing competition.
School uniforms are a really good idea that many people like.
My school has uniforms and I wear mine every day.
Some schools have uniforms and some schools do not.

W.explanation: A persuasive claim is specific and evidence-based. Option A makes a clear argument backed by a reason.

W.questionText: A student wants to SHOW rather than TELL that a character is disappointed. Which sentence is best?

options.text: He stared at his empty trophy shelf and slowly slid his participation ribbon into the drawer.
He was very disappointed that he did not win.
He felt sad and unhappy about what happened.
He did not get the trophy and that made him feel bad.

W.explanation: Strong narrative writing 'shows' emotion through actions and details. Option A reveals disappointment through specific imagery without stating the feeling.

W.questionText: A kindergarten student wants to write a sentence about their favorite animal. Which sentence tells the most information?

options.text: I like dogs because they are fluffy and they play with me.
I like dogs.
Dogs.
Dogs are an animal.

W.explanation: Option B shares a preference and gives two specific reasons — more informative than simply naming the animal.

W.questionText: A student is writing an opinion piece arguing the school cafeteria should offer more fruit options. Which sentence provides the strongest supporting reason?

options.text: Research shows students who eat fruit during the school day have better concentration in afternoon classes.
I personally think fruit is delicious and everyone would like it.
Some cafeterias already have fruit and students choose it sometimes.
Fruit is better than candy in my opinion.

W.explanation: A supporting reason in an opinion essay should be logical and evidence-based. Option C cites research with a specific, relevant benefit.

W.questionText: Which sentence best introduces a counterargument in a persuasive essay about homework?

options.text: Some people argue that homework reinforces learning, but research suggests that beyond a certain point, extra practice yields diminishing returns.
Homework is too hard and takes too long every night.
I agree with everyone who says homework is useful.
Homework should be eliminated because students are busy.

W.explanation: A counterargument acknowledges the opposing view ('some people argue') before refuting it — option A is the only one that does both.

W.questionText: A student's essay has this weak conclusion: 'In conclusion, those are my facts about dolphins.' Which revision is best?

options.text: Dolphins' remarkable intelligence, communication skills, and social bonds make them among the most fascinating animals in the ocean.
In conclusion, those were all the facts about dolphins.
Dolphins are mammals that live in the ocean.
That is the end of my report about dolphins.

W.explanation: A strong informative conclusion synthesizes key ideas, not just restates 'in conclusion.' Option B brings back the main themes of intelligence, communication, and social bonds.

W.questionText: A student is writing a story that begins: 'One morning, Lena found a tiny door behind the bookshelf.' What would make the BEST next sentence?

options.text: She pressed her ear against it and heard something that sounded exactly like tiny music.
The door was small. It was very small indeed.
This is a story about Lena and a door.
Doors can be many different sizes in different houses.

W.explanation: A strong narrative next sentence introduces new sensory detail and raises a question to pull readers forward — option C does both.

W.questionText: A student's argument lacks a clear claim. Which revision gives it the STRONGEST claim?

options.text: Schools should teach financial literacy because students who understand budgeting and saving make stronger economic decisions as adults.
Financial literacy is something some schools teach.
Money is important and everyone should know about it.
There are many different opinions about what schools should teach students.

W.explanation: A strong claim is specific, debatable, and supported by a reason — option D includes both a clear position and evidence-based rationale.

W.questionText: Which transition word or phrase best shows that the second sentence CONTRASTS with the first?

options.text: However
Furthermore
For example
In addition

W.explanation: 'However' signals a contrast or exception. 'Furthermore,' 'for example,' and 'in addition' all add or illustrate rather than contrast.

W.questionText: A student writes: 'My favorite color is blue.' What could they add to make it a stronger opinion sentence?

options.text: ...because it looks like the sky and the ocean, which are my two favorite things.
...and my friend likes red.
...blue is a color.
...I wrote this sentence about blue.

W.explanation: Adding a reason ('because') turns a simple statement into an opinion with support — the foundation of opinion writing.

W.questionText: Which sentence uses the most precise language to describe movement?

options.text: She sprinted across the finish line, arms pumping, lungs burning.
She ran fast across the finish line.
She moved quickly when she crossed the finish line.
She got to the finish line after running.

W.explanation: Precise language uses vivid verbs ('sprinted') and sensory details ('arms pumping, lungs burning') to put the reader in the scene.

W.questionText: A student is writing about recycling. Which sentence would BEST introduce a specific supporting detail?

options.text: For example, recycling one aluminum can saves enough energy to run a television for three hours.
Recycling is good for the environment in many ways.
People should recycle more often than they currently do.
Recycling is when you put bottles and cans in a special bin.

W.explanation: Supporting details in informative writing should be specific and factual — option B provides a concrete, quantified example.

W.questionText: Which revision makes this sentence clearer and more precise?  Original: 'The thing was really big and kind of scary looking.'

options.text: The storm cloud loomed over the valley, dark and swollen with rain.
The thing was very, very big and scary in an important way.
There was a big, scary thing that I saw.
It was quite large and somewhat frightening, I thought.

W.explanation: Replacing vague nouns ('thing') and weak modifiers ('really big') with specific nouns ('storm cloud') and concrete details creates precise, vivid writing.

W.questionText: A student is writing a rebuttal to the argument that athletes should not be required to maintain a grade point average. Which is the strongest rebuttal?

options.text: Academic eligibility requirements teach athletes that success in sports requires the same discipline — consistent effort, time management, and follow-through — demanded in the classroom.
I disagree with that position because I think grades are important.
Athletes should get better grades so they can keep playing sports.
Many people believe grade requirements are unfair to athletes.

W.explanation: A strong rebuttal doesn't just assert the opposite — it explains the reasoning. Option D connects athletic and academic discipline with a logical parallel.

SL.questionText: A student wants to share her idea during a class discussion. What should she do first?

options.text: Wait until another speaker finishes before raising her hand
Interrupt the speaker to share her idea right away
Whisper her idea to the person sitting next to her
Write a note and pass it to the teacher

SL.explanation: Collaborative discussion norms include taking turns — wait for the speaker to finish before raising your hand.

SL.questionText: Malik disagrees with a classmate's idea. Which response shows the best discussion skills?

options.text: "I understand your point, but I see it differently — the text says the character changed his mind before the ending."
"That's wrong. You didn't read it right."
"I don't want to talk about this anymore."
"Whatever, it doesn't matter what the text says."

SL.explanation: Effective discussion means acknowledging other perspectives respectfully while supporting your view with evidence.

SL.questionText: Which strategy would make Amara's presentation about climate change most effective?

options.text: Use specific facts and data, speak clearly, and make eye contact with the audience
Read every word directly from notes without looking up
Use as many technical words as possible to sound knowledgeable
Speak as quickly as possible to cover all the information

SL.explanation: Effective presentations combine accurate content with clear delivery and audience engagement through eye contact.

SL.questionText: Which strategy will best help a student evaluate a documentary about ocean pollution?

options.text: Notice what evidence is shown and consider whether the source seems reliable and unbiased
Accept all information in a documentary as accurate because it was professionally made
Focus only on the parts she personally agrees with
Take notes only on parts that are funny or entertaining

SL.explanation: Critical media literacy involves evaluating evidence quality and source reliability.

SL.questionText: A student has 10 minutes of content for a 3-minute presentation. What should she do?

options.text: Select the most important points and practice staying within the time limit
Speak as fast as possible to cover all content
Ask the teacher to extend her time to 10 minutes
Read all notes aloud even if it takes longer

SL.explanation: Effective presentations require prioritizing content and managing time — selecting key points to fit the limit.

SL.questionText: 'I see what you mean, but I'd push back on that because the data shows the opposite.' What does this response demonstrate?

options.text: Acknowledging a peer's argument while using evidence to respectfully disagree
Changing the topic to avoid the disagreement
Refusing to participate productively in the discussion
Agreeing with the peer while pretending to disagree

SL.explanation: This shows advanced discussion skills: acknowledging the peer's point while offering a counter-argument with evidence.

SL.questionText: When someone is talking to you, what is the polite thing to do?

options.text: Look at them and listen carefully without interrupting
Look around the room while they speak
Start talking about something different
Walk away if the topic is not interesting

SL.explanation: Active listening means giving eye contact and attention — it shows respect and helps you understand what's being said.

SL.questionText: A student is not sure what her classmate means. What is the BEST thing to say?

options.text: "Can you explain what you mean by that?"
"That doesn't make any sense."
Say nothing and wait for the teacher to explain
Pretend she understands and say 'okay'

SL.explanation: Asking a clarifying question shows engagement and helps conversation move forward productively.

SL.questionText: A student has been assigned a group discussion role as 'discussion leader.' What is her MAIN job?

options.text: Make sure everyone has a chance to share, keep the discussion focused, and draw out key ideas
Share the longest and most detailed response so others can learn from her
Take all the notes and present the group's answer to the class
Decide which ideas are correct and tell others when they are wrong

SL.explanation: A discussion leader facilitates — ensuring inclusion, focus, and synthesis — not dominating or judging contributions.

SL.questionText: A student watches a video advertisement for a new sports drink. What should she think about when evaluating the message?

options.text: Who made the ad, what they want her to do, and whether the claims are supported by evidence
Whether the music in the ad sounds good
Whether the athlete in the ad is someone she recognizes
Only whether the product looks like something her friends would use

SL.explanation: Media literacy means identifying the creator's purpose, intended audience, and checking whether claims are evidence-based.

SL.questionText: A student is giving a formal argument speech about reducing plastic use. Which choice of language is MOST appropriate?

options.text: "Research indicates that single-use plastics constitute approximately 40 percent of plastic waste annually."
"Plastic is, like, really bad for the environment and stuff."
"Honestly, I just think plastic is kind of gross and we should stop using it."
"Everyone knows that plastic is the worst thing ever for the ocean."

SL.explanation: Formal academic speech uses precise language, evidence, and avoids filler words or vague claims — option C does all three.

SL.questionText: A student listens to a read-aloud about the lifecycle of a butterfly. Afterward, what is the BEST way to show she understood?

options.text: Retell the main stages in order — egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly
Say she liked the story and ask for a different one
Draw a picture of her favorite part only
Read the book again on her own

SL.explanation: Demonstrating listening comprehension means retelling key information in sequence — the hallmark of active listening.

SL.questionText: During a Socratic seminar, a student wants to build on what another classmate just said. Which response shows the BEST discussion skills?

options.text: "I want to build on what Marcus said — if the theme is really about belonging, then the ending makes even more sense when..."
"Actually, what Marcus said is wrong. The theme is something completely different."
"I agree with Marcus" (and nothing else)
"Let me talk about my own idea, which is totally different from Marcus's."

SL.explanation: Building on a peer's idea ('I want to build on what Marcus said') demonstrates collaborative thinking and advances the group's understanding.

SL.questionText: A teacher reads a passage about earthquakes aloud. What is the BEST note-taking strategy during the read-aloud?

options.text: Write down key words and the most important facts as they are mentioned
Write down every word the teacher says
Wait until the end to write down what you remember
Draw a picture of the Earth to help remember

SL.explanation: Effective note-taking during listening captures key words and important facts in real time — too little loses information, too much is impossible.

SL.questionText: A student adds images and a graph to her presentation on rising ocean temperatures. How do these visuals strengthen her argument?

options.text: They make the data visible and help audiences understand the scale of change that words alone cannot convey
They distract the audience from any weaknesses in her spoken argument
They replace the need to cite sources or use evidence
They make the presentation longer, which shows more effort

SL.explanation: Multimedia in presentations serves a rhetorical purpose — making abstract data visible and emotionally resonant, which reinforces the argument.

SL.questionText: Your teacher asks: 'What did the story say the bear did in winter?' What should you do to answer well?

options.text: Think back to what you heard in the story and say what the bear did in your own words
Guess any answer and hope it is right
Say you don't remember and ask to read the book
Ask a friend for the answer before you respond

SL.explanation: Answering a listening comprehension question means recalling and retelling information from the spoken text in your own words.

SL.questionText: Before a class discussion, students read the same article. Why does the teacher assign this preparation?

options.text: So everyone has shared knowledge and can back up their ideas with evidence from the text
So the teacher does not need to explain the topic during discussion
So students who read faster can help students who are slower
Because reading the same article means everyone will reach the same conclusion

SL.explanation: Shared text preparation ensures all participants can contribute substantively and cite specific evidence — a foundation for productive academic discussion.

SL.questionText: What distinguishes a productive academic debate from an unproductive argument?

options.text: A debate uses evidence and logic to engage with opposing views; an argument often relies on emotion or personal attacks
In a debate, one person always wins; in an argument, there is no winner
A debate is always formal; an argument always happens informally
Arguments use evidence; debates rely only on personal opinion

SL.explanation: Academic debate is characterized by evidence-based reasoning and engagement with counterarguments — not emotional escalation or personal attacks.

SL.questionText: A student is asked to tell the class about her weekend. Which response uses the most complete spoken sentence?

options.text: On Saturday, my family went to the farmer's market and I tried strawberry lemonade for the first time.
The market. Lemonade.
We went somewhere.
Yeah, um, it was fun, I think.

SL.explanation: A complete spoken sentence includes a subject, verb, and specific information. Option A tells who, when, what, and an interesting detail.

SL.questionText: A student listens to a classmate's report on the civil rights movement. What should she think about when evaluating the presentation?

options.text: Whether the speaker used accurate information, organized ideas clearly, and communicated them in a way the audience could understand
Whether the speaker is her friend or someone she likes
Whether the topic is interesting to her personally
Whether the speaker finished before the time limit

SL.explanation: Evaluating a speaker means assessing content accuracy, organization, and audience communication — not personal preferences or timing alone.

L.questionText: Which sentence uses capitalization correctly?

options.text: Last summer, we visited the Grand Canyon in Arizona.
Last Summer, we visited the grand canyon in arizona.
last summer, we visited the Grand canyon in arizona.
Last summer, we visited the Grand Canyon in arizona.

L.explanation: Proper nouns (Grand Canyon, Arizona) are capitalized; common nouns and seasons (summer) are not.

L.questionText: Which sentence is written correctly?

options.text: The children ran quickly to the playground after lunch.
The childrens ran quick to the playground after lunch.
The children runned quickly to the playground after lunch.
The children ran quick to the playground after lunch.

L.explanation: 'Children' is an irregular plural; 'ran' is the correct past tense of 'run'; 'quickly' is the correct adverb form.

L.questionText: Which sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement?

options.text: The team of players is ready for the championship.
The team of players are ready for the championship.
The team of players were ready for the championship.
The team of players have been ready for the championship.

L.explanation: The subject is 'team' (singular collective noun), so it takes the singular verb 'is.'

L.questionText: 'The classroom was a zoo after the bell rang.' What type of figurative language is this?

options.text: Metaphor
Simile
Personification
Hyperbole

L.explanation: A metaphor directly compares two unlike things without 'like' or 'as.' Calling the classroom 'a zoo' is a metaphor.

L.questionText: 'Benevolent' contains the root 'bene' meaning 'good.' What does 'benevolent' most likely mean?

options.text: Kind and generous toward others
Strict and demanding in attitude
Confused or uncertain about a decision
Loud and forceful in speech

L.explanation: Knowing 'bene' means 'good' points toward a positive meaning — 'benevolent' means kind or generous.

L.questionText: Which sentence uses a noun correctly?

options.text: The cat sat on the warm mat.
The quickly cat sat on the mat.
Cat the sat on mat the.
The cat sat on warm the mat.

L.explanation: Nouns name people, places, or things and must be used in correct grammatical position. Option A correctly places nouns in subject and object positions.

L.questionText: 'Her concise answer left no room for confusion.' Which word is closest in meaning to 'concise'?

options.text: brief and clear
long and detailed
loud and confident
unusual and creative

L.explanation: 'Concise' means expressing a lot in a few words — brief and clear.

L.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?

options.text: The concert was sold out; we bought tickets online the night before.
The concert; was sold out we bought tickets online.
The concert was sold out we; bought tickets online.
The; concert was sold out we bought tickets online.

L.explanation: Semicolons connect two independent clauses. Option A correctly places the semicolon between two complete, related thoughts.

L.questionText: Which sentence contains a simile?

options.text: Her laugh was like a bell ringing on a clear morning.
Her laugh was a bell ringing on a clear morning.
The bell rang loudly in the morning.
She laughed loudly during the clear morning.

L.explanation: A simile uses 'like' or 'as' to compare two unlike things. Option A compares a laugh to a bell using 'like.'

L.questionText: 'Portable' comes from the Latin 'portare' meaning 'to carry.' Which word uses the same root?

options.text: transport
important
report
support

L.explanation: 'Transport' contains the root 'port' (to carry) — transporting means carrying something across a distance.

L.questionText: Which sentence names one thing and one action correctly?

options.text: The dog runs.
Run the dog.
Dog the run.
Runs dog.

L.explanation: A complete sentence needs a subject (the dog) and a verb (runs) in the correct order — subject before verb.

L.questionText: Which sentence uses a capital letter and ending punctuation correctly?

options.text: My dog loves to run in the park.
my dog loves to run in the park.
My dog loves to run in the park
my dog loves to run in the park

L.explanation: Sentences begin with a capital letter and end with a period (or other ending punctuation).

L.questionText: Which sentence uses a verb in the past tense?

options.text: She walked to school this morning.
She walks to school every day.
She will walk to school tomorrow.
She is walking to school right now.

L.explanation: 'Walked' is the simple past tense. 'Walks' is present, 'will walk' is future, 'is walking' is present progressive.

L.questionText: Read the sentence: 'The stars winked at us from the dark sky.' What type of figurative language is used?

options.text: Personification
Simile
Metaphor
Onomatopoeia

L.explanation: Personification gives human qualities to non-human things. Stars cannot wink — assigning that human action to them is personification.

L.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an intensive pronoun?

options.text: She herself painted the entire mural.
Herself painted the entire mural.
She painted the entire herself mural.
She painted the entire mural and herself.

L.explanation: Intensive pronouns (myself, herself, himself) immediately follow the noun they intensify. Option C places 'herself' immediately after 'She' to emphasize she did it alone.

L.questionText: A student encounters the word 'anticlimactic' in a text. Which strategy would BEST help determine its meaning?

options.text: Break it into prefix (anti-), root (clim-), and suffix (-actic) and use knowledge of each part
Replace it with a word she already knows and see if the sentence still makes sense
Skip the word and assume the sentence still makes sense without it
Look at only the last three letters to identify its word family

L.explanation: Morpheme analysis (breaking words into prefix, root, suffix) is the most systematic vocabulary strategy for unfamiliar academic words.

L.questionText: Which sentence uses a correlative conjunction correctly?

options.text: Either Marcus will present first, or Aisha will.
Either Marcus will present first or Aisha will present first or neither.
Both Marcus and Aisha will present, but neither are ready.
Neither Marcus or Aisha is ready to present today.

L.explanation: Correlative conjunctions come in pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and. 'Either...or' is correctly used in option B.

L.questionText: Which sentence uses the word 'bark' to mean the outer covering of a tree?

options.text: The bark of the old oak tree was deeply grooved and rough to the touch.
The dog began to bark loudly at the mail carrier.
'Bark!' said the puppy, wagging its tail.
She could hear the dog bark from three houses away.

L.explanation: Context determines which meaning of a homonym is intended. 'Bark of the old oak tree' clearly refers to the tree covering, not the dog sound.

L.questionText: A student wants to write the same information in a more formal style. Which revision is best?

options.text: The research indicates that regular physical activity significantly improves academic performance.
Studies show exercise is really good for doing well in school, which is pretty cool.
Exercise and school grades go together, according to some people who study things.
Basically, if you exercise, you might do better at school, which is neat.

L.explanation: Formal academic writing avoids filler words ('really,' 'basically,' 'pretty cool') and uses precise, neutral language — option D does this consistently.

L.questionText: A student reads: 'The senator's equivocal response frustrated reporters who wanted a direct answer.' Based on context, what does 'equivocal' mean?

options.text: Unclear and open to multiple interpretations; deliberately evasive
Strongly worded and impossible to misunderstand
Politely worded to avoid causing offense
Based on careful research and expert consultation

L.explanation: Reporters were frustrated because they wanted a 'direct answer' — implying the equivocal response was the opposite: unclear or evasive.
